newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Farmers urge end to Aboriginal title uncertainty.
newsitem.headline: Farmers urge end to Aboriginal title uncertainty.

text.p: Australia's row over Aboriginal land rights came to a head on Friday when a farm leader called on Prime Minister John Howard to demand that farmers and miners be guaranteed exclusive occupancy on their leases.

National Farmers' Federation president Don McGauchie told reporters on his way to Howard's Sydney office that if farmers and miners did not get back exclusive rights to their land, Australia's economic interests would be greatly harmed.

"This will be enormously expensive for this country. Whatever happens this country is going to lose some of its growth, some of its jobs, it's going to cost us a great deal of money," he said. Minerals and farm products, the two frontline sectors of the Australian economy which might be hurt by a December High Court ruling that native title could co-exist with pastoral and mining leases, underpin much of Australia's commodities-geared economy.

In the 1996/97 fiscal year ending June 30, the value of farm output is officially estimated at A$20.3 billion ($15.4 billion), while the value of mineral output is forecast at A$36.3 billion. Much of the output of both sectors is exported, particularly to Asia.
Mineral output would be hit before farm production but Australia's farming activities already were being affected by the title uncertainty, McGauchie said.
On the land, feelings run deeply over a native title ruling of the High Court, Australia's highest court, in December.

In a split decision, the High Court ruled in a claim by the Wik aboriginal group over 35,000 square km (14,000 square miles) of land in north Queensland that a pastoral lease did not automatically extinguish Aboriginal land claims.

Describing the matter as one of the most difficult problems Australia has ever faced, McGauchie said on Friday that only legislation, not judicial votes in an unrepresentative High Court, could resolve the matter.
McGauchie emerged from his meeting with Howard subdued but declaring himself "very happy" with "a preliminary discussion".
Further talks would be held, more detail would be put into proposals, and Howard would meet in coming weeks with Australian mine and Aboriginal groups, he said.
"We agreed with the Prime Minister that while we want a quick solution, we don't want a quickie solution," he said. "Ninteen ninety-seven has to be the year in which we fix it."

The Queensland state government had said that much new development work now cannot be approved, he said, while in other parts of the country, development applications have not been processed because of concern over title clarity.
Farmer concern is heightened by the fact that about 42 percent of Australia's vast area is covered by pastoral leases.

The NFF is calling on the government to ensure validation for all freehold, residential, commercial and agricultural leases and public works. They want cities, townsites, land and water resources quarantined from native title.
The farmer lobby's views do not strike a full accord Australia-wide.

Aboriginal groups have argued that the High Court decision, which dealt with the right of natives to hunt and hold tribal ceremonies on pastoral land if they could prove a connection with that land, would not harm pastoral activities.
